root.stem: A 31-year-old woman comes to the clinic 6 weeks after delivering her third child. For the past 5 weeks she has felt sad and tearful most of the day, has lost interest in activities she used to enjoy, including sex, and has trouble concentrating. She wakes at 4 AM every morning and cannot fall back asleep, has lost 4 kg (9 lb) without trying, and feels guilty that she is not enjoying her baby. She says her family would be better off without her. She has had two similar episodes in the past, each lasting several months with full recovery in between, and has never had a period of unusually high energy, decreased need for sleep, or racing thoughts. She also reports vague cramping abdominal pain, and an abdominal ultrasound last week was normal. She has no hallucinations or unusual beliefs about the baby. Her examination, thyroid-stimulating hormone level, and complete blood count are normal, and she does not drink alcohol or use drugs.

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A mood disorder with low mood or loss of interest that impairs function. The clincher: **depressed mood or loss of interest nearly every day, with 5 or more of 9 symptoms (depressed mood, loss of interest, sleep change, guilt or worthlessness, low energy, poor concentration, appetite or weight change, psychomotor change, thoughts of death), and never a manic or hypomanic episode**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Also written as major depression or clinical depression. 'Unipolar' means mood moves in one direction only: there are no manic episodes.

nodes.q: How long must the symptoms last before the diagnosis can be made?
nodes.note: At least 5 of the 9 symptoms (mnemonic SIGECAPS: Sleep, Interest, Guilt, Energy, Concentration, Appetite, Psychomotor, Suicidal thoughts, plus depressed mood) nearly every day, and one must be depressed mood or loss of interest (anhedonia). Tearfulness lasting less than 2 weeks after a birth fits the postpartum blues instead.

nodes.q: Which neurotransmitters are low in the monoamine hypothesis?
nodes.note: Antidepressants raise monoamine levels in the synapse. The hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis is also overactive, with high cortisol, and imaging shows reduced prefrontal activity.

nodes.q: On a sleep study, how is the time from falling asleep to her first rapid eye movement (REM) sleep period changed?
nodes.note: REM sleep begins early and is increased, with less slow-wave (deep) sleep; this fits her early morning waking.

nodes.q: Which specifier fits the timing of her illness?
nodes.note: In the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, fifth edition, text revision (DSM-5-TR): onset during pregnancy or in the **4 weeks after delivery**. Her symptoms began about 1 week after birth.

nodes.q: Once she recovers, she asks when her risk of another episode would be highest if she had a fourth child. What do you tell her?
nodes.a: After delivery (the postpartum period), more than during pregnancy
nodes.note: Depression during pregnancy can often be treated safely. A woman in remission with past episodes still carries extra risk, so she should not be told her risk is normal.

nodes.q: Before her mood was asked about, her abdominal pain and weight loss had led only to normal tests. What should come before any further gut imaging or endoscopy?
nodes.a: Evaluation for depression (a clinical interview, with a screening questionnaire such as the Patient Health Questionnaire-9, PHQ-9)
nodes.note: Unexplained physical complaints, weight loss, fatigue and sleep change point to depression; evaluate for it before more fiber, a barium enema, or repeat imaging or colonoscopy after normal results.

nodes.q: She says her family would be better off without her. What must you ask her next?
nodes.a: Whether she has thoughts of death or of killing herself
nodes.note: Asking does not plant the idea. Avoid empty reassurance ('you will feel better soon') or treating it as normal new-mother stress. Ask every depressed patient, including a withdrawn teenager who only complains of abdominal pain; in children and teenagers irritable mood can replace sad mood.

nodes.q: A 32-year-old man sleeps 11 hours a night, has gained weight, enjoys nothing, and is tired with poor concentration. He has the same illness. Which depressive specifier does his sleep and weight pattern point to?
nodes.note: **Mood reactivity** (mood brightens with good events) plus two of: weight gain or increased appetite, oversleeping, a heavy leaden feeling in the limbs, and long-standing sensitivity to rejection. It is still major depressive disorder, not antisocial personality disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder, posttraumatic stress disorder or somatic symptom disorder. Monoamine oxidase inhibitors work well, but selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors are used first.

nodes.q: A 66-year-old man has had erectile dysfunction, fatigue, and poor sleep and concentration since a stroke 3 months ago. Which libido and nocturnal-erection pattern points to depression as the cause?
nodes.a: Decreased libido with normal nocturnal erections
nodes.note: Depression lowers sexual interest while the physical mechanism stays intact, so nighttime and morning erections persist. Normal libido with lost nocturnal erections points to a vascular, neurologic or hormonal cause. Depression is common after a stroke.

nodes.q: What is first-line treatment for a moderate to severe episode?
nodes.a: A selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) plus psychotherapy such as cognitive behavioral therapy
nodes.note: Sertraline is a usual choice when breastfeeding. Response starts after 2 to 4 weeks, with full effect by 6 to 8 weeks. Continue 6 to 12 months after remission; with three episodes, long-term maintenance is advised.

nodes.q: How do SSRIs work?
nodes.a: They block the presynaptic serotonin reuptake transporter, raising serotonin in the synapse
nodes.note: Fluoxetine, sertraline and paroxetine are examples. Adverse effects: sexual dysfunction, gastrointestinal upset, hyponatremia in older adults, and serotonin syndrome if combined with a monoamine oxidase inhibitor.

nodes.q: Where do the serotonin neurons that the drug acts on arise?
nodes.note: Locus ceruleus neurons make norepinephrine; the substantia nigra makes dopamine.

nodes.q: Why is a tricyclic antidepressant a poor choice in a depressed patient with a recent heart attack and a long PR interval?
nodes.a: It blocks cardiac sodium channels (quinidine-like), slowing conduction and causing arrhythmias
nodes.note: Paroxetine, an SSRI, is the safe choice among the usual options; sertraline is the best studied after a heart attack. Alprazolam and buspirone treat anxiety, carbamazepine is a mood stabilizer, and haloperidol and methylphenidate do not treat this depression. Tricyclics are also lethal in overdose (convulsions, coma, cardiotoxicity) and cause anticholinergic effects and orthostatic hypotension.

nodes.q: Which treatment is reserved for severe, psychotic, suicidal or treatment-resistant depression?
nodes.note: Works fast and is safe in pregnancy; main adverse effects are transient memory loss and confusion.

nodes.q: Her tearfulness after delivery could be the postpartum blues. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Tearfulness and mood swings **in the first days, peaking by day 3 to 5, gone by 2 weeks**; no loss of function and no suicidal thoughts; reassurance only
**Five or more symptoms lasting over 2 weeks, with loss of interest, guilt and impaired function**

nodes.note: The trap: both begin after delivery and bring tears and poor sleep.

nodes.q: Her depressive episodes could belong to bipolar disorder. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **At least one manic episode** (a week of high energy, little need for sleep, racing thoughts); bipolar II needs a hypomanic episode
**Depressive episodes only; she has never had high energy, less need for sleep or racing thoughts**

nodes.note: Ask every depressed patient about past mania: an antidepressant given alone can switch bipolar disorder into mania.

root.stem: A 27-year-old man is found unresponsive on a bathroom floor by his roommate, with a rubber tourniquet loosely around his left arm and a syringe beside him. He opens his eyes only to a painful stimulus and does not speak, giving a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 7. His pulse is 46/min, respirations are 6/min and shallow, blood pressure is 92/58 mm Hg, and rectal temperature is 35.8°C (96.4°F). His pupils are 1 mm and equal, there is no odor of alcohol, and old needle tracks line both forearms. His fingerstick glucose is normal, and bowel sounds are decreased.
root.oneliner: 27M + found unresponsive with tourniquet and syringe + Glasgow Coma Scale score 7 + pulse 46, respirations 6/min and shallow, blood pressure 92/58, temperature 35.8°C + pupils 1 mm + no alcohol odor + old needle tracks + normal glucose + decreased bowel sounds

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Overdose of an opioid such as heroin, morphine, fentanyl or oxycodone. The clincher: **pinpoint pupils + slow shallow breathing + decreased level of consciousness**, often with needle tracks. Pulse, blood pressure, temperature, bowel sounds and the Glasgow Coma Scale score all fall; a score of 8 or less means the airway is at risk.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Both names describe the same toxidrome; 'opioid toxicity' is also used.

nodes.q: Why are his pupils so small?
nodes.a: Opioids disinhibit the Edinger-Westphal nucleus, increasing parasympathetic output through the oculomotor nerve to the pupillary sphincter
nodes.note: Tolerance does not develop to miosis or constipation, so they persist in long-term users. Pupils can dilate if severe hypoxia follows.

nodes.q: Activation of which opioid receptor causes the slow breathing?
nodes.note: Mu receptors in the brainstem make the respiratory centers less sensitive to rising carbon dioxide. Mu also mediates analgesia, euphoria, miosis, constipation and dependence. Kappa causes spinal analgesia and dysphoria; delta contributes to analgesia; sigma is not a true opioid receptor.

nodes.q: What is the main cause of death?
nodes.note: Unrecognized hypoventilation leads to hypoxic brain injury and cardiac arrest. Aspiration and non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema can follow.

nodes.q: Which lung complication can follow the overdose?
nodes.note: Fluid leaks into the alveoli despite a normal heart.

nodes.q: What confirms the diagnosis at the bedside?
nodes.a: Rapid improvement in breathing and alertness after naloxone
nodes.note: Check glucose and the rest of the vital signs at once. A urine drug screen may miss fentanyl and many synthetic opioids, so do not wait for it.

nodes.q: What is the immediate treatment?
nodes.a: Airway support and ventilation, then naloxone
nodes.note: Naloxone can be given intravenously, intramuscularly or intranasally and repeated. Watch him in a monitored setting.

nodes.q: How does naloxone reverse the overdose?
nodes.a: It is a competitive antagonist at the mu opioid receptor
nodes.note: It has no effect in someone who is not on opioids.

nodes.q: Why can he become sedated again hours later?
nodes.a: Naloxone wears off after about 30 to 90 minutes, sooner than many opioids
nodes.note: The risk is highest with long-acting opioids such as methadone. Observe for several hours and repeat or infuse naloxone.

nodes.q: If he is physically dependent, what appears right after naloxone?
nodes.a: Precipitated withdrawal: yawning, runny nose, dilated pupils, goosebumps, cramps and diarrhea
nodes.note: Uncomfortable but rarely life-threatening, unlike alcohol or barbiturate withdrawal.

nodes.q: Stupor and slow breathing could suggest benzodiazepine intoxication. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Normal-sized pupils**; sedation and slurred speech, with breathing usually affected only if combined with alcohol or opioids; flumazenil reverses it
**Pinpoint pupils + respirations around 6/min + needle tracks**; naloxone reverses it

nodes.note: The trap: both depress consciousness and breathing, but benzodiazepines alone rarely stop breathing and leave the pupils normal.

root.stem: A 14-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department because she suddenly could not stand or walk 4 days ago, the morning after she failed an important exam. Her parents are visibly anxious, but she describes her legs calmly and seems unconcerned. She is afebrile, with a pulse of 72/min. Muscle bulk, tone and deep tendon reflexes in the legs are normal and symmetric, and plantar responses are flexor. She cannot lift either leg against resistance on the bed, yet she moves both legs normally when distracted while changing her clothes. Sensation to pinprick in the legs differs from one examination to the next and follows no nerve or dermatome pattern. She has had no recent infection or vaccination, and magnetic resonance imaging of the spine is normal. She denies hallucinations, flashbacks, feeling detached from herself, or worry about having a serious illness.

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: One or more neurologic symptoms (weakness, paralysis, blindness, loss of sensation, seizure-like attacks) that do not fit any known neurologic disease and are not faked. The clincher: **a sudden motor or sensory deficit with normal reflexes and an examination that is inconsistent, such as normal movement when distracted**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: This is the name in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, fifth edition, text revision (DSM-5-TR), with conversion disorder in brackets.

nodes.q: Which named bedside sign tests whether her leg weakness is functional?
nodes.note: When she lifts one leg against resistance, the 'weak' leg pushes down normally into the bed. Like her normal movement when distracted, it shows **inconsistency with neurologic disease**, which DSM-5-TR requires. A psychological stressor is common but no longer required.

nodes.q: Without her knowing it, her paralysis spares her from facing her failed exam. What is this unconscious benefit called?
nodes.note: Secondary gain is an outside benefit, such as attention or missing school. She is not pretending: deliberate faking to take on the sick role is factitious disorder, and faking for an external reward is malingering.

nodes.q: What is her calm attitude toward her symptoms called?
nodes.note: Classic but unreliable; many patients with the disorder are distressed, and some with organic disease seem indifferent.

nodes.q: What is the best management?
nodes.a: Reassurance that the symptoms are real and reversible, with physical therapy and psychotherapy
nodes.note: Do a full neurologic examination and make the diagnosis from positive signs of inconsistency; avoid confrontation and repeated invasive tests. Physical therapy and cognitive behavioral therapy help. Most sudden-onset cases resolve in days to weeks.

nodes.q: Which features predict a good outcome?
nodes.a: Sudden onset, a clear stressor and a short time before treatment
nodes.note: Long-standing symptoms, immobility (contractures, muscle wasting) and other psychiatric illness predict a poor outcome.

nodes.q: Being unable to walk could suggest Guillain-Barre syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

**Normal reflexes, no wasting, and strength that returns when she is distracted**

nodes.note: The trap: the main organic mimic that you must exclude when a child cannot walk.

The skin is red, dry and flaky, and it does not itch or hurt. Over the same period he has lost 3 kg (6.6 lb), eats less, and his grades have fallen from As to Cs; his father says he seems forgetful and tired. Hydrocortisone cream had no effect. Vital signs are normal. He has no cough, blood in the urine, diarrhea, or hair loss, and no one else at home has a rash.

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Deliberately breathing in fumes of volatile solvents (paint, glue, gasoline, aerosols) to get high, usually in early adolescence. The clincher: **a steroid-resistant perioral rash with paint residue on the nostrils and fingers in a young adolescent whose school performance is falling**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Inhalant use disorder is the term in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, fifth edition, text revision; the practice is called huffing, sniffing or bagging, and the rash 'glue-sniffer's rash'.

nodes.q: Which solvent in paint and glue is most often responsible?
nodes.note: Others include butane, propane, gasoline and aerosol propellants. Nitrous oxide is a different inhalant: it inactivates vitamin B12 and causes subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord. Amyl nitrite ('poppers') causes methemoglobinemia.

nodes.q: How do these solvents produce the high?
nodes.a: Central nervous system depression: they enhance gamma-aminobutyric acid type A receptor activity and block N-methyl-D-aspartate receptors, like alcohol
nodes.note: Euphoria and dizziness come within seconds and last minutes, so users inhale repeatedly. Dopamine release in the reward pathway adds to the effect.

nodes.q: Why does the skin around his nose and mouth break out?
nodes.a: Repeated contact with solvent that strips the skin's fats, causing irritant dermatitis
nodes.note: Hence it fails to respond to steroid cream and appears where the rag, bag or can touches the face.

nodes.q: Which fatal event can happen even with first-time use?
nodes.note: Solvents sensitize the myocardium to catecholamines, so a startle or exertion after use can trigger ventricular fibrillation.

nodes.q: Which kidney problem follows chronic toluene exposure?
nodes.a: Distal (type 1) renal tubular acidosis with hypokalemia
nodes.note: A non-anion-gap metabolic acidosis with low potassium and low phosphate; hippuric acid, the toluene metabolite, is found in the urine.

nodes.q: Which long-term brain damage can follow?
nodes.a: Cerebellar ataxia and cognitive decline from white-matter damage
nodes.note: Poor memory and falling grades are early clues; n-hexane also causes a peripheral neuropathy.

nodes.q: How do you support the diagnosis?
nodes.a: A confidential adolescent interview, with urine hippuric acid and a metabolic panel
nodes.note: Standard urine drug screens miss solvents. Check electrolytes including potassium, renal function and an electrocardiogram.

nodes.q: What is the management?
nodes.a: Stop exposure, give counseling with family involvement, and treat the complications; there is no antidote
nodes.note: Avoid epinephrine during an arrhythmia; a beta-blocker is preferred. Screen for depression and other drug use.

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Sudden psychosis (delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech or behavior) that clears completely. The clincher: **psychotic symptoms lasting 1 day to less than 1 month in a previously healthy person, with a full return to baseline**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: The older term for a psychotic episode that follows severe stress; in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, fifth edition, text revision (DSM-5-TR) it is the specifier 'with marked stressor(s)'.

nodes.q: How long may the episode last?
nodes.a: At least 1 day but less than 1 month
nodes.note: Lasting 1 to 6 months it becomes schizophreniform disorder, and 6 months or more is schizophrenia.

nodes.q: Which event in his story is the kind of trigger that can start it?
nodes.a: A major stressor such as the death of a parent
nodes.note: Other triggers are childbirth (postpartum onset) or catastrophic events; it can also occur with no stressor, and is commoner with personality disorders.

nodes.q: Which causes must be excluded first?
nodes.a: Substance intoxication and medical or neurologic illness
nodes.note: Check a urine drug screen, glucose, electrolytes, thyroid tests and head imaging; a normal result supports a primary psychiatric disorder. Confirm no mood episode.

nodes.q: What is the treatment?
nodes.a: Short-term antipsychotic medication in a safe setting, with supportive therapy
nodes.note: Admit if he is a danger to himself or others, because paranoia and voices can lead to suicide or violence. Benzodiazepines can calm agitation. Taper after the episode and follow up for relapse.

nodes.q: Which receptor do these drugs block to reduce the voices?
nodes.a: Dopamine D2 receptors in the mesolimbic pathway
nodes.note: Antipsychotics treat hallucinations and delusions, not apathy.

nodes.q: What is the usual outcome?
nodes.a: Full recovery, though some later prove to have schizophrenia or a mood disorder
nodes.note: Relapse is possible, so follow-up matters.

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Unwanted, repeated thoughts and rituals that take over daily life. The clincher: **intrusive fears that drive repeated rituals, taking hours a day, which she recognizes as excessive**. Pregnancy and the postpartum period can trigger or worsen it, as here.

nodes.q: Apart from distress or impairment, how much daily time spent on symptoms makes them time-consuming enough to qualify?
nodes.a: More than 1 hour a day, or significant distress or impairment
nodes.note: Rituals or obsessions that cause clinically significant distress or impairment also qualify. She spends over 2 hours a day.

nodes.q: She knows her fears are excessive. What term describes symptoms that feel unwanted and foreign to the person?
nodes.note: She has good insight; the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, fifth edition, text revision (DSM-5-TR) specifiers are good or fair, poor, and absent insight. In obsessive-compulsive personality disorder the traits feel right to the person (ego-syntonic).

nodes.q: Which brain circuit is overactive?
nodes.a: The cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical loop (orbitofrontal cortex and caudate nucleus)
nodes.note: Serotonin signaling in this circuit is abnormal, which is why serotonergic drugs work. Tic disorders such as Tourette syndrome often co-occur. In children, sudden onset after streptococcal infection is called pediatric autoimmune neuropsychiatric disorders associated with streptococcal infections (PANDAS).

nodes.q: Her repeated washing feels as though it cancels the harm she fears for the baby. Which defense mechanism is this?
nodes.note: Isolation of affect and reaction formation are the other defenses classically linked with obsessive-compulsive disorder.

nodes.q: What is first-line treatment?
nodes.a: A selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) such as sertraline, with exposure and response prevention (a form of cognitive behavioral therapy)
nodes.note: Higher doses than for depression and 8 to 12 weeks are needed to judge a response. Alprazolam, haloperidol, lithium, methylphenidate and the monoamine oxidase inhibitor phenelzine are not first-line.

nodes.q: Which tricyclic antidepressant is also effective because it strongly blocks serotonin reuptake?
nodes.note: Reserved for SSRI failure because of anticholinergic effects, seizures and cardiac toxicity.

root.stem: A 33-year-old man tells his physician that he wants help to stop smoking cannabis. Over 3 years he has gone from smoking a few times a week to smoking all day. He often uses far more than he plans and has tried at least five times to cut down without success. He spends hours each day obtaining and using it, craves it intensely at work, and was fired last month for repeated absences. He has given up weekend basketball with friends, and his girlfriend has threatened to leave, but he continues to use. He now needs about four times as much to get the same effect, and when he stops he becomes irritable and cannot sleep for several days. He has no hallucinations or delusions, and his examination is normal.
root.oneliner: 33M + wants to stop smoking cannabis + 3 years from a few times a week to all day + uses more than planned + five failed attempts to cut down + hours daily obtaining and using + craving + fired for absences + gave up basketball + girlfriend threatens to leave but continues + needs 4 times as much + irritable and insomnia when stopping + no psychosis
highlight: tried at least five times to cut down without success
fired last month for repeated absences
needs about four times as much
irritable and cannot sleep for several days

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.a: Cannabis use disorder (a substance use disorder)
nodes.note: A pattern of compulsive use despite harm. The clincher: **loss of control over use, craving, failed attempts to cut down, and continued use despite harm to work and relationships**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: The older term; the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, fifth edition, text revision (DSM-5-TR) merged 'abuse' and 'dependence' into one disorder graded by severity.

nodes.q: How many criteria are needed to make the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Out of 11 criteria; the same criteria apply to every substance.

nodes.q: Using his criteria, how severe is his disorder?
nodes.note: Mild is 2 to 3, moderate 4 to 5, severe 6 or more. He meets nine: larger amounts, failed cutting down, time spent, craving, failed role at work, relationship problems, activities given up, tolerance and withdrawal.

nodes.q: What is his need for four times as much cannabis to get the same effect called?
nodes.note: His irritability and insomnia on stopping are withdrawal. These two are the pharmacologic criteria, and neither is required for the diagnosis. Cannabis withdrawal also brings anxiety, restlessness, low appetite and low mood.

nodes.q: Activation of which neurotransmitter pathway explains the rewarding effect shared by cocaine, opioids, alcohol, nicotine and cannabis?
nodes.a: The dopamine reward pathway (ventral tegmental area to nucleus accumbens to prefrontal cortex)
nodes.note: Exam options may word it as dopaminergic neurons from the nucleus accumbens to the prefrontal cortex. Cocaine blocks dopamine reuptake and amphetamine releases dopamine, while opioids, alcohol, nicotine and cannabinoids increase firing of ventral tegmental neurons. Noradrenergic locus ceruleus, endorphin and gamma-aminobutyric acid pathways are not the shared reward pathway.

nodes.q: Which change in striatal dopamine receptors helps explain why he has given up basketball and ordinary pleasures?
nodes.a: Fewer D2 receptors in the striatum, so ordinary rewards feel less pleasurable
nodes.note: Chronic use blunts reward from natural rewards and drives craving.

nodes.q: Which brain region, underactive in addiction, weakens control over use despite consequences?
nodes.note: It handles judgment and impulse control; cue-driven craving is triggered through the amygdala.

nodes.q: Through which receptor does tetrahydrocannabinol, the main active ingredient of cannabis, act in the brain?
nodes.note: A presynaptic Gi protein-coupled receptor that reduces release of other neurotransmitters, indirectly raising dopamine in the reward pathway. Dronabinol, a synthetic tetrahydrocannabinol, treats chemotherapy nausea and anorexia in acquired immunodeficiency syndrome.

nodes.q: Which severe mental illness is heavy adolescent cannabis use linked to?
nodes.note: He has no psychotic symptoms now.

nodes.q: He asks for help to stop. Which stage of change is he in?
nodes.note: He is ready and planning to change. Stages: precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action, maintenance, with relapse possible at any point.

nodes.q: What is the foundation of treatment?
nodes.a: Motivational interviewing and cognitive behavioral therapy, with contingency management
nodes.note: No drug is approved for cannabis use disorder. For other substances, medicines help: buprenorphine or methadone for opioids, naltrexone for alcohol, varenicline for nicotine. Screen for co-occurring depression and anxiety.

nodes.q: Cannabis intoxication is a separate cannabis diagnosis. How do you tell it from his disorder?

split.note: A **reversible state within 2 hours of use**: euphoria, impaired judgment, red eyes, fast pulse, dry mouth and increased appetite
**A pattern over 12 months of loss of control, craving, tolerance and harm to work and relationships**; his examination is normal now

nodes.note: The trap: intoxication is an acute effect that anyone who uses can have, not a disorder.

root.stem: A 52-year-old man is admitted for a hip fracture after a fall at home. About 30 hours after admission he has a generalized tonic-clonic seizure lasting one minute, with no focal deficits afterwards. Soon after, he is shaking, drenched in sweat and says that insects are crawling on the walls. He knows his name, the date and the hospital. Pulse is 118/min, blood pressure is 164/98 mm Hg, temperature is 37.5°C and respirations are 16/min. Pupils are 4 mm and reactive, eye movements are full without nystagmus, and he recalls the events of the past day. Serum sodium is 139 mEq/L and potassium is 3.0 mEq/L. He has received morphine for pain since admission. His wife says he drinks about a pint of whiskey every day.
root.oneliner: 52M + hip fracture admission + generalized tonic-clonic seizure at 30 hours + tremor, sweating, pulse 118, blood pressure 164/98 + insects on the walls with a clear sensorium + potassium 3.0 + daily whiskey drinker

insects are crawling on the walls
knows his name, the date and the hospital
Pulse is 118/min, blood pressure is 164/98 mm Hg
eye movements are full without nystagmus
recalls the events of the past day
drinks about a pint of whiskey every day

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: The nervous system rebounds when a heavy drinker stops abruptly. The clincher: **shaking, sweating, fast pulse and high blood pressure with a seizure or hallucinations 1 to 3 days after the last drink, often after admission to hospital**.

nodes.q: How many hours after the last drink do withdrawal seizures usually occur?
nodes.note: Tremor and anxiety start at 6 to 24 hours. Hallucinations also appear at 12 to 48 hours.

nodes.q: Which type of seizure is typical?
nodes.a: Generalized tonic-clonic, with no focal findings
nodes.note: Usually one or a few brief seizures. A focal finding should prompt a search for another cause such as a head injury. Phenytoin does not prevent or treat alcohol withdrawal seizures; a benzodiazepine does.

nodes.q: If 48 to 96 hours after the last drink he became disoriented, feverish and fluctuating in consciousness, what would this severe form be called?
nodes.note: DSM-5-TR calls it alcohol withdrawal delirium. It is the dangerous end of withdrawal: autonomic instability, and death from arrhythmia, hyperthermia or cardiovascular collapse (mortality up to about 5% even with treatment). It is treated in the intensive care unit with benzodiazepines.

nodes.q: Visual hallucinations with a clear sensorium and normal orientation during withdrawal are called what?
nodes.note: DSM-5-TR records it as alcohol withdrawal with perceptual disturbances. Begins at 12 to 48 hours and usually settles within days. Hallucinations are mostly visual or tactile. Orientation and attention stay intact, which separates it from delirium tremens.

nodes.q: Why does stopping alcohol overactivate the nervous system?
nodes.a: Alcohol's boost of GABA-A receptors is lost while glutamate (NMDA) activity stays high and noradrenaline surges
nodes.note: Chronic alcohol use down-regulates GABA-A receptors and up-regulates NMDA receptors. Removing alcohol leaves the brain with too little inhibition.

nodes.q: What is the main reason his potassium is low?
nodes.a: A catecholamine surge shifts potassium into cells
nodes.note: Adrenaline and noradrenaline stimulate beta-2 receptors and the sodium-potassium pump. Poor intake, vomiting and diarrhea add to it.

nodes.q: Which other electrolyte must be checked and replaced because low levels keep potassium low?
nodes.note: Magnesium is usually low in heavy drinkers. Potassium will not correct until it is replaced.

nodes.q: Which scale measures severity and guides dosing?
nodes.a: Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol, revised (CIWA-Ar)
nodes.note: Doses are given by symptom score. Scores above 8 to 10 call for a benzodiazepine.

nodes.q: Which drug class is first-line, given right away?
nodes.a: Benzodiazepines (for example intravenous diazepam or lorazepam)
nodes.note: They control the autonomic signs and prevent seizures and delirium tremens.

nodes.q: How do benzodiazepines act on the GABA-A receptor?
nodes.a: They increase how often the chloride channel opens
nodes.note: Barbiturates increase how long the channel stays open. Both need GABA to be present at low doses.

nodes.q: Which benzodiazepines are preferred in most patients, and why?
nodes.a: Long-acting ones (chlordiazepoxide, diazepam), because they taper themselves and give smoother control
nodes.note: Their active metabolites fall slowly, so there are fewer breakthrough seizures.

nodes.q: If he had cirrhosis or were frail and elderly, which benzodiazepines would you choose?
nodes.note: They are cleared by conjugation without active metabolites, so they do not build up in a failing liver.

nodes.q: Which vitamin is given before any glucose-containing fluid?
nodes.note: It prevents Wernicke encephalopathy, which glucose alone can precipitate in a thiamine-depleted drinker.

nodes.q: His brain symptoms could suggest Wernicke encephalopathy. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Confusion + ataxia + eye-movement abnormality (nystagmus or ophthalmoplegia)** from thiamine deficiency; no seizure or autonomic storm
**Seizure + hallucinations + tremor, sweating, fast pulse and high blood pressure; eyes move normally**

nodes.q: His hospital confusion could suggest Korsakoff syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Anterograde amnesia with confabulation** in an alert patient; no autonomic signs and no seizures
**Intact memory for recent events with tremor, sweating and a seizure** soon after admission

nodes.note: DSM-5-TR names it alcohol-induced major neurocognitive disorder, amnestic-confabulatory type.

nodes.q: His seizure could suggest hyponatremia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Serum sodium usually below 120 mEq/L**, often after vomiting, water intake or a drug; no tremor or sweating
**Normal sodium (139 mEq/L) with autonomic overactivity** in a daily drinker

nodes.q: His seizure could suggest a complex partial seizure. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Aura, staring, lip smacking or automatisms with impaired awareness**; starts in one temporal lobe and he would not be oriented afterward
**Tonic-clonic from the start with no focal onset**, plus tremor, sweating and a high pulse

nodes.q: His fear, sweating and fast pulse could suggest panic disorder. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Discrete attacks of fear peaking within minutes, with fear of dying**; no hallucinations or seizure; no link to stopping a substance
**Hallucinations and seizure 1 to 2 days after the last drink, with tremor and persistent sweating**

nodes.note: The trap: both give a fast pulse, sweating and anxiety.

nodes.q: His fast pulse and sweating could suggest sepsis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Fever, low blood pressure and a source of infection**; the pulse is fast but the pressure is falling
**High blood pressure, tremor and hallucinations with only a low-grade temperature**

nodes.q: The morphine he has received could suggest an opioid effect. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Sedation, small pupils and slow breathing**
**Pupils 4 mm, respirations 16/min, with agitation and a high pulse and blood pressure**

nodes.note: Morphine also does not cause seizures or hallucinations at ordinary doses.

For 2 weeks she has slept about 2 hours a night but says she has never felt more energetic. Her speech is rapid and hard to interrupt, and she has run up three credit cards buying gifts for strangers. She says a divine voice gives her instructions. She was treated for major depressive disorder 6 years ago. She began drinking a bottle of wine each evening 1 week ago, after the sleepless nights began. Pulse is 88/min, blood pressure is 124/78 mm Hg, there is no tremor, and urine toxicology and thyroid-stimulating hormone are normal.

a divine voice gives her instructions

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Mood disorder defined by at least one manic episode. The clincher: **at least 1 week of elevated, expansive or irritable mood with high energy and little need for sleep** (any length if hospitalization is needed).

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: The older name. Exam options often simply say bipolar disorder, sometimes with the specifier (manic, with psychotic features).

nodes.q: How long must the elevated mood and energy last to call it a manic episode?
nodes.a: At least 7 days, or any length if hospitalization is needed
nodes.note: Hypomania needs only 4 days and no psychosis or hospitalization, which makes bipolar II disorder.

nodes.q: Her voice and her belief about leading the country occur only during the mood episode. How is that recorded?
nodes.a: As a specifier: manic episode with psychotic features
nodes.note: The diagnosis stays bipolar I disorder. Her grandiose themes are mood-congruent. Psychosis rules out hypomania: any psychotic feature makes the episode manic.

nodes.q: Before an antidepressant is started alone for depression, what must you ask about?
nodes.a: Any past manic or hypomanic episode
nodes.note: An antidepressant without a mood stabilizer can trigger mania. Her earlier depression may have been the first episode of this illness.

nodes.q: Which tests are used to rule out a substance-induced or medical cause?
nodes.note: Also review medications, steroids and alcohol use. Stimulants and hyperthyroidism can both mimic mania.

nodes.q: What is first-line treatment for acute mania with psychotic features?
nodes.a: A mood stabilizer (lithium or valproate) plus an atypical antipsychotic
nodes.note: Olanzapine, risperidone or quetiapine act fastest on agitation and psychosis. A benzodiazepine can be added for sleep and agitation.

nodes.q: Which long-term mood stabilizer has a narrow therapeutic range and needs blood levels checked?
nodes.note: It inhibits inositol monophosphatase and so depletes inositol in neurons. Adverse effects: tremor, hypothyroidism, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and Ebstein anomaly in pregnancy. Thiazides, NSAIDs and ACE inhibitors raise levels.

nodes.q: Which complication causes the most deaths in this disorder?
nodes.note: Risk is highest in depressive and mixed episodes, so ask about it at every visit.

nodes.q: Her voice and delusions could suggest schizophrenia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Psychosis for at least 6 months, flat affect and disorganization** with no prominent mood episodes
**Psychosis only during a week-long episode of high energy and little sleep**

nodes.note: The trap: both can have grandiose delusions and voices.

nodes.q: Her psychosis could suggest schizoaffective disorder. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Delusions or hallucinations for at least 2 weeks with no mood episode**, while mood episodes are present for most of the illness
**Psychosis only while the mood is elevated**

nodes.q: Her sudden psychosis could suggest brief psychotic disorder. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Psychosis lasting 1 day to under 1 month with no mood episode**, often after a stressor
**Psychosis within a manic episode of 1 week or more, with decreased need for sleep**

nodes.q: Her fixed belief could suggest delusional disorder. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Non-bizarre delusions for at least 1 month** with otherwise intact functioning and no manic episode
**Grandiose delusions only with manic mood, pressured speech and little sleep**

nodes.q: Her wine intake could suggest alcohol withdrawal. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Tremor, sweating, fast pulse and high blood pressure after stopping heavy drinking**; hallucinosis is perceptual only
**Sleeplessness began before the drinking; she is still drinking, with a normal pulse and pressure and no tremor**

nodes.q: Her mood swings could suggest cyclothymic disorder. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **At least 2 years of hypomanic and depressive symptoms that never meet full episode criteria**
**A full manic episode with psychosis**

eaten very large amounts of food in under an hour about three times a week
calluses over the backs of her right knuckles

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: An eating disorder of people at normal or above-normal weight. The clincher: **recurrent binge eating followed by compensatory vomiting, laxatives or fasting, with weight in the normal range**.

nodes.q: How often must binges and compensatory behaviors occur to meet the criteria?
nodes.a: At least once a week for 3 months
nodes.note: Her self-esteem is also unduly tied to body shape. If this happens only during anorexia nervosa, that diagnosis is made instead.

nodes.q: Which salivary glands enlarge from repeated vomiting?
nodes.note: Painless swelling of both cheeks (sialadenosis) with a raised serum amylase of salivary origin.

nodes.q: Besides enamel erosion, which dental problem does repeated vomiting make more likely?
nodes.note: Gastric acid erodes enamel from the tongue side of the upper teeth (perimylolysis), which leaves them prone to decay and sensitivity.

nodes.q: What causes the calluses on the backs of her knuckles?
nodes.a: Scraping against the incisors while inducing vomiting (Russell sign)
nodes.note: A classic sign of self-induced vomiting.

nodes.q: Which potassium and acid-base pattern follows repeated vomiting?
nodes.note: Vomiting loses hydrogen chloride and volume, so the kidneys waste potassium. Laxative abuse instead gives a metabolic acidosis with low potassium.

nodes.q: Which complication of this disorder can kill?
nodes.note: The ECG shows flat T waves, U waves and a prolonged QT interval. Management (step 2): replace potassium and magnesium and monitor the ECG.

nodes.q: What is first-line treatment?
nodes.note: It targets the binge-purge cycle and distorted body image. Hospitalization is for arrhythmia, severe electrolyte disturbance or suicidal thoughts.

nodes.q: Which drug is approved for this disorder?
nodes.a: Fluoxetine, a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI), at higher doses (60 mg)
nodes.note: Added to cognitive behavioral therapy. Bupropion is avoided because it lowers the seizure threshold.

nodes.q: Her vomiting and laxatives could suggest anorexia nervosa, binge-purge type. How do you tell them apart?

**Normal weight (BMI 23) with regular menses, normal pulse and normal body hair**

nodes.note: The trap: both involve purging and distorted body image; the weight separates them.

nodes.q: Her binges could suggest binge eating disorder. How do you tell them apart?

**Binges followed by self-induced vomiting and laxatives**

nodes.q: Her fatigue could suggest hypothyroidism. How do you tell them apart?

**Normal reflexes and pulse with a normal thyroid; swollen cheeks and enamel loss**

nodes.q: Her headaches could suggest a prolactinoma (prolactin-secreting pituitary adenoma). How do you tell them apart?

root.stem: A 78-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by police after she was found wandering in a parking lot. She says, "I feel fine, leave me alone," and refuses an examination. She is oriented to herself only and cannot repeat three digits backward. She falls asleep during the interview and then wakes alert and angry. No one accompanies her, but a neighbor tells the police she was chatting normally three days ago. A pharmacy bag in her coat holds a receipt for sertraline started 9 days ago. Temperature is 37.0°C and pulse is 82/min. Mucous membranes are mildly dry. There are no focal deficits, tremor or clonus. Serum sodium is 122 mEq/L.

falls asleep during the interview and then wakes alert and angry
no focal deficits, tremor or clonus

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: An acute brain failure from a medical cause. The clincher: **acute onset over hours to days with fluctuating attention and awareness, and disorientation**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Also called acute encephalopathy.

nodes.q: Which cognitive function is most disturbed?
nodes.note: She cannot hold attention to repeat digits. Memory, language and perception are affected as well. It must not be better explained by an existing dementia. Electroencephalography, if done, shows diffuse slowing.

nodes.q: Which electrolyte disturbance is the likely cause here?
nodes.note: Sodium of 122 mEq/L after a new selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) in an older woman. Delirium is often multifactorial, so also look for infection, dehydration, drugs and hypoxia.

nodes.q: What mechanism explains the low sodium from the SSRI?
nodes.a: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH)
nodes.note: Excess antidiuretic hormone retains water and dilutes the sodium. Older women on SSRIs are at highest risk. Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion needs euvolemia, so her mildly dry mouth means volume status must be checked (urine osmolality and urine sodium); poor intake can add to the low sodium.

nodes.q: She refuses help and cannot give a history. What is the best next step?
nodes.a: Obtain collateral information from family or caregivers
nodes.note: The history of onset, medications and baseline function is what separates delirium from dementia. Do not sedate or discharge her.

nodes.q: What is the core treatment?
nodes.a: Find and correct the underlying cause
nodes.note: Here: stop the SSRI and correct the sodium slowly (no more than about 8 mEq/L in 24 hours), since fast correction risks osmotic demyelination.

nodes.q: Which measures come first for agitation?
nodes.a: Non-drug measures: reorientation, glasses and hearing aids, a quiet room with day-night cues
nodes.note: Avoid restraints and urinary catheters where possible.

nodes.q: If agitation endangers her or staff, which drug is used?
nodes.note: Short course at the lowest dose: older patients are sensitive to its side effects, and the QT interval should be watched.

nodes.q: Which drug class commonly worsens delirium and is avoided apart from alcohol or sedative withdrawal?
nodes.note: They add sedation and paradoxical agitation. Anticholinergics are also avoided.

nodes.q: Her confusion could suggest Alzheimer dementia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Insidious, gradual memory loss over years with stable attention and alertness**
**Acute onset over days with fluctuating attention and arousal**

nodes.note: The trap: both cause disorientation in an older patient; the tempo and attention separate them. DSM-5-TR calls it major neurocognitive disorder due to Alzheimer disease.

nodes.q: Her new SSRI could suggest serotonin syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Fever, clonus, hyperreflexia, diarrhea and agitation within about 24 hours of starting or raising a serotonergic drug**
**Normal temperature, no clonus or tremor, and low sodium**

nodes.q: Her behavior could suggest Pick disease (frontotemporal dementia). How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Early personality change, disinhibition and language loss, usually before age 65**, with Pick bodies; slow progression
**Acute change with fluctuating attention in a 78-year-old**

nodes.q: Her confusion could suggest vascular dementia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Stepwise decline with risk factors and focal neurologic deficits**
**Abrupt global change with no focal deficits and a reversible metabolic cause**

nodes.q: Her refusal and agitation could suggest a primary psychosis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Intact orientation and attention with fixed delusions or hallucinations**; no fluctuating arousal
**Disoriented, inattentive and drowsy at times, with a medical cause**

root.stem: A 51-year-old woman comes for a follow-up visit. For many years she has worried about her health, money and her children's safety, cannot stop the worry even when nothing is wrong, and feels on edge, tired and tense with poor sleep. She has taken alprazolam daily for 12 years and declines to see a psychiatrist, saying she feels better and trusts this physician more. Over the past 2 days the office received 12 calls from her about minor symptoms and her medication doses. She lives with her husband, makes her own decisions and works as a bookkeeper. She has never had sudden attacks of intense fear. Pulse is 74/min, her weight is stable and thyroid-stimulating hormone is normal.

cannot stop the worry even when nothing is wrong
on edge, tired and tense with poor sleep
12 calls from her about minor symptoms and her medication doses
never had sudden attacks of intense fear

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Chronic, hard-to-control worry about many everyday matters. The clincher: **excessive worry on most days for at least 6 months, about several areas, with restlessness, fatigue, tension and poor sleep**.

nodes.q: For how long must the worry be present?
nodes.note: It must be hard to control and out of proportion to the actual risks.

nodes.q: At least how many of the six associated symptoms are needed in an adult?
nodes.note: Restlessness, fatigue, poor concentration, irritability, muscle tension, sleep disturbance.

nodes.q: Which drug class is first-line for long-term treatment?
nodes.a: A selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) or serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (such as escitalopram or venlafaxine)
nodes.note: Combine with cognitive behavioral therapy. Benefit takes 2 to 6 weeks.

nodes.q: Which non-sedating anxiolytic without dependence risk is an alternative?
nodes.a: Buspirone, a partial agonist at serotonin 1A receptors
nodes.note: It takes 2 to 4 weeks to work, so it does not help in an acute attack. No sedation, no dependence and no effect on the GABA-A receptor.

nodes.q: What is the concern with her 12 years of alprazolam?
nodes.a: Tolerance and dependence, with rebound anxiety and seizures if stopped abruptly
nodes.note: Alprazolam is short-acting and potent, so interdose rebound and withdrawal are marked. Benzodiazepines are for short-term bridging only; taper slowly if stopping. Falls and cognitive impairment rise with age.

nodes.q: She calls the office many times a day. What is the best approach?
nodes.a: Set clear limits on phone calls and schedule regular office visits
nodes.note: This gives the reassurance she needs in a predictable way. Do not refuse her care or dismiss her calls, and do not force psychiatric referral.

nodes.q: Her frequent calls could suggest dependent personality disorder. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Pervasive need to be taken care of, submissiveness, and inability to make everyday decisions without reassurance**; fears being left alone
**Worry across many domains with restlessness and tension, while she makes her own decisions**

nodes.note: The trap: both seek reassurance; the decision-making and the worry separate them.

nodes.q: Her anxiety could suggest panic disorder. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Recurrent unexpected attacks peaking in minutes, with palpitations and fear of dying**, then worry about more attacks
**Constant background worry with no discrete attacks**

nodes.q: Her tension could suggest hyperthyroidism. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Weight loss, heat intolerance, tremor and low thyroid-stimulating hormone**
**Stable weight and normal thyroid-stimulating hormone**

nodes.q: Her calls about minor symptoms could suggest illness anxiety disorder. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Preoccupation with having or getting one serious illness for at least 6 months**, with few or no physical symptoms
**Worry spread across health, money and her children's safety**, with tension, fatigue and poor sleep

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A lifelong pattern of social inhibition from feelings of inadequacy. The clincher: **avoids people because of fear of rejection or criticism, yet wants relationships and is at ease with a few close contacts**.

nodes.q: Which three themes define the pattern?
nodes.a: Social inhibition, feelings of inadequacy and hypersensitivity to negative evaluation
nodes.note: Four or more of seven listed features are needed, such as avoiding jobs that need contact and holding back in intimate relationships for fear of shame.

nodes.q: Which personality disorder cluster does it belong to?
nodes.note: Cluster C also holds dependent and obsessive-compulsive personality disorders.

nodes.q: What does he expect will happen if he joins in?
nodes.note: He wants closeness, which is the opposite of the indifference in schizoid personality disorder.

nodes.q: What is the main treatment?
nodes.a: Psychotherapy: cognitive behavioral therapy, social skills training and group therapy
nodes.note: A selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor can be added if social anxiety is also present.

nodes.q: His few friends could suggest schizoid personality disorder. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Content alone with no wish for closeness and no fear of judgment**
**Longs for relationships but avoids them from fear of rejection**

nodes.note: The trap: both are socially isolated; the wish for company separates them.

nodes.q: His discomfort around people could suggest social anxiety disorder. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Fear of specific social or performance situations such as public speaking, without a pervasive sense of being inadequate**
**Lifelong, pervasive avoidance with a core view of himself as inept**

nodes.note: The two overlap heavily; the pervasive self-image distinguishes the personality disorder.

nodes.q: His withdrawal could suggest schizotypal personality disorder. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Odd beliefs, magical thinking, ideas of reference and eccentric speech**
**Normal thinking and speech with fear of rejection**

nodes.q: His wariness could suggest paranoid personality disorder. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Distrust that others will harm or exploit him**
**Believes others will reject him, not harm him**

nodes.q: His social difficulty could suggest antisocial personality disorder. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Disregard for others' rights, deceit, impulsivity and no remorse**
**Anxious and overly sensitive to criticism, with no rule-breaking**

root.stem: A 22-year-old man is brought to the clinic by his sister because of 8 months of withdrawal and strange behavior. He was a strong engineering student but stopped attending classes, no longer bathes, and wears stained clothes. He says his neighbors hid cameras in the walls to track his thoughts, and he hears a voice commenting on everything he does. During the interview he speaks little, in short sentences, and stops mid-sentence as if listening to someone. A urine drug screen is negative. He has never had a period of unusually high or low mood. His uncle was treated for a similar illness. His sister is in tears and asks what is happening to her brother.
root.oneliner: 22M + 8 months of withdrawal + stopped attending classes, stopped bathing + cameras in the walls tracking his thoughts + voice commenting on his actions + speaks little, short answers, stops mid-sentence + negative urine drug screen + no mood episodes + uncle with similar illness + tearful sister

hears a voice commenting on everything he does
stops mid-sentence as if listening to someone
never had a period of unusually high or low mood

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A chronic psychotic illness with loss of function. The clincher: **delusions and hallucinations with a clear decline in function, lasting 6 months or more, without a mood episode or drug cause**.

nodes.q: How long must the illness last before the diagnosis is made?
nodes.a: At least 6 months, including at least 1 month of active symptoms
nodes.note: DSM-5-TR needs 2 or more of: delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, grossly disorganized or catatonic behavior, negative symptoms. At least one must be delusions, hallucinations or disorganized speech. Function at work, school or self-care falls well below the earlier level.

nodes.q: His hallucinations are auditory, the most typical type in this illness. Which type would instead point first to delirium?
nodes.note: Voices commenting on his actions or talking to each other are classic for schizophrenia. Tactile hallucinations (bugs under the skin) suggest cocaine or amphetamine use or alcohol withdrawal; olfactory hallucinations suggest a temporal lobe seizure aura.

nodes.q: Besides his sparse speech, which emotional finding is his mental status examination most likely to show?
nodes.note: Negative symptoms: flat affect, poverty of speech, loss of drive, loss of pleasure, social withdrawal. They respond poorly to first-generation drugs. He stays alert and oriented, and his memory is intact, unlike in delirium or dementia.

nodes.q: Which inheritance pattern does the family history follow?
nodes.a: Multifactorial (many genes plus environment, with no Mendelian pattern)
nodes.note: Risk is about 10% with an affected first-degree relative and about 50% in an identical twin. The pedigree looks like that of type 1 diabetes mellitus, another multifactorial disease.

nodes.q: Which neurotransmitter change is thought to cause the positive symptoms?
nodes.a: Excess dopamine activity in the mesolimbic pathway
nodes.note: Low dopamine in the mesocortical pathway is linked to the negative symptoms. Imaging often shows enlarged lateral ventricles and less gray matter.

nodes.q: Which receptor do antipsychotic drugs block to treat the positive symptoms?
nodes.note: Second-generation drugs also block serotonin 5-HT2A receptors, which causes fewer movement side effects.

nodes.q: Days after starting a high-potency D2 blocker, which life-threatening reaction causes high fever, lead-pipe rigidity, confusion and a very high creatine kinase?
nodes.note: Dopamine blockade in the hypothalamus and basal ganglia. Stop the drug; give dantrolene or bromocriptine. Muscle breakdown releases myoglobin, which can cause **acute kidney injury**.

nodes.q: After years of D2 blockade, which movement disorder causes involuntary lip-smacking and tongue movements?
nodes.note: Thought to come from upregulated, supersensitive D2 receptors in the striatum. It is often irreversible; valbenazine or deutetrabenazine (VMAT2 inhibitors) can help. Earlier effects: acute dystonia (hours to days), akathisia (days to weeks), parkinsonism (weeks).

nodes.q: He fails two antipsychotics and starts clozapine. Which blood problem requires regular neutrophil counts?
nodes.note: Clozapine also lowers suicide risk in schizophrenia and can cause seizures, myocarditis and weight gain.

nodes.q: What is first-line treatment?
nodes.a: An oral second-generation antipsychotic such as risperidone, plus psychosocial support
nodes.note: Long-term treatment lowers relapse risk. Check weight, glucose and lipids because of metabolic side effects.

nodes.q: Which formulation helps a patient who often stops taking tablets?
nodes.note: Stopping medication is the most common cause of relapse.

nodes.q: His sister is crying. Which first response by the physician is most appropriate?
nodes.a: Acknowledge her distress, then ask an open-ended question about what she has noticed
nodes.note: Respond to the emotion first, then gather the history. Do not announce a diagnosis, blame drugs or stress, or lecture about hygiene before listening.

nodes.q: Which cause of death is most tied to the illness itself?
nodes.note: About 5 to 10% of patients die by suicide, mostly in the first years after onset.

nodes.q: His symptoms could suggest schizophreniform disorder. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Same symptoms, but **lasting 1 to 6 months**; function may stay intact
**Symptoms for 6 months or more** with clear loss of function

nodes.note: The trap: only the duration separates them.

nodes.q: His symptoms could suggest brief psychotic disorder. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Psychosis lasting 1 day to under 1 month**, then full return to baseline
**Eight months of symptoms** with decline that does not reverse

nodes.q: His voice and beliefs could suggest bipolar I disorder with psychotic features. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Psychosis appears **only during manic or depressive episodes**; a mood episode with sleeplessness, grandiosity or low mood is present
**Psychosis and decline without any mood episode**, and a flat rather than elevated mood

nodes.q: His psychosis could suggest schizoaffective disorder. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Major mood episodes present for most of the illness, plus **psychosis for 2 weeks or more without any mood episode**
**No mood episode at any time**; psychosis and decline alone

nodes.q: His hallucinations could suggest a substance-induced psychotic disorder. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Starts during or soon after use of a drug such as amphetamine, cannabis or phencyclidine (PCP) and **clears within weeks of stopping; urine drug screen is positive**
**Negative drug screen and symptoms persisting for months**

nodes.q: His fixed beliefs could suggest delusional disorder. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Delusions for 1 month or more with no other psychotic symptoms**; hallucinations, if any, are not prominent, and function apart from the delusion is preserved
**Hallucinations, negative symptoms and marked decline in function** besides the delusions

nodes.q: His odd beliefs could suggest schizotypal personality disorder. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Lifelong **eccentric behavior, magical thinking and social anxiety without frank psychosis**; function preserved
**True hallucinations and fixed delusions with a clear drop from prior function**

nodes.q: His suspicion of his neighbors could suggest borderline personality disorder. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Brief, stress-related paranoid ideas** with unstable relationships, self-harm and fear of abandonment
**Persistent hallucinations and fixed delusions for months** with withdrawal

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A neurodevelopmental disorder of inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity. The clincher: **inattentive and hyperactive-impulsive behavior since early childhood that causes problems in more than one setting**.

nodes.q: By what age must the symptoms have started?
nodes.note: Symptoms must last at least 6 months and be out of keeping with the child's developmental level.

nodes.q: In how many settings must the symptoms cause impairment?
nodes.a: At least two (for example home and school)
nodes.note: Symptoms at school only suggest a problem with the classroom, teacher or a learning disorder instead.

nodes.q: Which neurotransmitters are underactive in the prefrontal circuits of these children?
nodes.note: Poor attention and impulse control follow from low catecholamine signalling in the frontal cortex and basal ganglia.

nodes.q: What is the net effect on these neurotransmitters of the drug class most likely to help him?
nodes.a: More dopamine and norepinephrine released into the synapse
nodes.note: Amphetamine increases their release; methylphenidate mainly blocks their reuptake. Both raise synaptic catecholamines. Benzodiazepines such as alprazolam (gamma-aminobutyric acid, GABA), selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) such as fluoxetine, and monoamine oxidase inhibitors such as tranylcypromine do not treat the core symptoms; sodium-channel blockers are anticonvulsants.

nodes.q: Which drug is first-line for a school-age child?
nodes.note: Combine with behavioral therapy and parent training. For children under 6, start with parent training in behavior management alone.

nodes.q: Which side effect of stimulants most often slows a child's weight gain and growth?
nodes.note: Also insomnia, raised heart rate and blood pressure, and worsening of tics. Check height, weight and blood pressure at follow-up.

nodes.q: If stimulants fail or are not tolerated, which selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor is an alternative?
nodes.note: Alpha-2 agonists such as guanfacine and clonidine are other non-stimulant options. Atomoxetine has no abuse potential.

nodes.q: Which consequence of his symptoms has already harmed him?
nodes.a: Accidental injuries from impulsive, risky play
nodes.note: Children with this disorder have more fractures, burns and emergency visits. Later risks are school failure and substance use.

nodes.q: His behavior could suggest oppositional defiant disorder. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Angry, argumentative, vindictive defiance toward authority figures**; attention is not the main problem
**Cannot sit still or finish tasks, but is polite and tries to follow rules**

nodes.note: The trap: both bring a child to the school office.

nodes.q: His risky acts could suggest conduct disorder. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Deliberate violation of others' rights**: bullying, cruelty to animals, stealing, fire-setting
**Impulsive and careless, not cruel**; injuries come from heedless play

nodes.q: His social trouble in class could suggest autism spectrum disorder. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Poor eye contact, delayed or odd speech, restricted interests and rigid routines**
**Normal speech, eye contact and play**; the problem is attention and activity level

nodes.q: His unfinished worksheets could suggest a specific learning disorder. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Difficulty with **reading, writing or math even when focused and working one-on-one**
**Reads at grade level one-on-one**, but loses focus and leaves tasks unfinished in class

root.stem: A 17-year-old girl who is a competitive gymnast is brought to the emergency department after fainting at practice. Her mother says she eats very little, has not had a period for 5 months, and exercises 3 hours every day. The girl says she feels 'still too fat' and is terrified of gaining weight. She is 166 cm tall and weighs 41 kg (body mass index 14.9 kg/m2). Pulse is 48/min and blood pressure is 86/54 mm Hg. Fine, downy hair covers her forearms, her skin is dry, and there are scars across the knuckles of her right hand and worn enamel on the back of her teeth. She denies heat intolerance or tremor. Serum potassium is 2.8 mEq/L, chloride 91 mEq/L and bicarbonate 35 mEq/L; arterial pH is 7.49 and PCO2 is 46 mm Hg. Urine chloride is 70 mEq/L.

scars across the knuckles of her right hand
worn enamel on the back of her teeth

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Restricted eating that leads to a significantly low body weight. The clincher: **low body weight + intense fear of gaining weight + distorted body image** (she still feels 'too fat').

nodes.q: Which two psychological features must accompany the low weight?
nodes.a: Intense fear of gaining weight (or behavior that keeps preventing weight gain) and a disturbed perception of her own body weight or shape
nodes.note: DSM-5-TR no longer requires amenorrhea. Severity in adults is rated by body mass index (BMI): mild 17 or above, moderate 16 to 16.99, severe 15 to 15.99, extreme below 15. In adolescents, BMI percentiles for age are used.

nodes.q: Which subtype does she have?
nodes.note: Purging by vomiting, laxatives or diuretics in the last 3 months. In the restricting type, weight loss comes only from dieting, fasting and exercise.

nodes.q: Which acid-base and potassium disturbance do her labs show?
nodes.note: Volume loss raises aldosterone, which wastes potassium and hydrogen ions in the urine; vomiting also loses stomach acid. The lungs retain CO2 to compensate (PCO2 46).

nodes.q: Besides vomiting, which substance is she most likely misusing, given her high urine chloride?
nodes.note: Loop or thiazide diuretics waste chloride in the urine while they act. Vomiting alone gives a low urine chloride (under 20 mEq/L) because the kidney holds on to chloride.

nodes.q: Her low potassium could suggest laxative misuse. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Diarrhea loses bicarbonate: **non-anion-gap metabolic acidosis** with low potassium
**Metabolic alkalosis** with low potassium and low chloride

nodes.note: Both lower potassium; the pH separates them.

nodes.q: What causes the scars across her knuckles?
nodes.a: Self-induced vomiting (teeth scraping the back of the hand)
nodes.note: This is Russell sign. Worn enamel and parotid swelling come from the same cause.

nodes.q: Which skin finding comes from starvation?
nodes.note: Dry skin and cold intolerance also appear.

nodes.q: Her thyroid tests would most likely show which pattern?
nodes.a: Low triiodothyronine (T3) with a normal thyroid-stimulating hormone
nodes.note: Euthyroid sick syndrome: starvation slows conversion of thyroxine to T3 and shifts it to reverse T3. It is an adaptation, not a reason to give thyroid hormone.

nodes.q: What causes her missed periods?
nodes.a: Energy deficiency suppresses hypothalamic gonadotropin-releasing hormone, so gonadotropins and estradiol fall
nodes.note: Luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone stay low (functional hypothalamic amenorrhea). Low estradiol also causes bone loss.

nodes.q: Which test screens for the long-term bone loss?
nodes.note: Low estrogen and high cortisol cause osteopenia or osteoporosis. Weight restoration is the main treatment; estrogen replacement does not restore bone well.

nodes.q: Which complication is the usual cause of death in severe cases?
nodes.a: Cardiac arrhythmia (sudden death), from low potassium and a prolonged QT interval
nodes.note: Bradycardia and low blood pressure reflect starvation. Suicide is the other major cause of death.

nodes.q: Her fainting, pulse of 48/min and potassium of 2.8 mEq/L call for which setting of care?
nodes.note: Other triggers: heart rate under 50 by day, systolic blood pressure under 90, orthostatic changes, severe electrolyte disturbance, or failed outpatient care. Get an electrocardiogram (ECG), electrolytes, magnesium and phosphate.

nodes.q: Which life-threatening problem can appear when feeding is restarted?
nodes.a: Refeeding syndrome, led by low phosphate
nodes.note: Insulin released by carbohydrate feeding drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells. Low phosphate depletes ATP, causing heart failure, arrhythmia, muscle weakness and breakdown. Increase calories slowly.

nodes.q: What is the main treatment for an adolescent?
nodes.note: Medication is not the foundation of treatment. SSRIs do not help at a low weight.

nodes.q: Which antidepressant is contraindicated in patients who purge?
nodes.note: It lowers the seizure threshold, a danger with electrolyte shifts from vomiting.

nodes.q: Her vomiting could suggest bulimia nervosa. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Normal or high body weight** with recurrent binge eating followed by compensatory behavior
**Body weight significantly low (body mass index 14.9)**; she restricts food

nodes.note: The trap: both purge and both have electrolyte disturbances. Anorexia nervosa is the diagnosis whenever weight is significantly low.

nodes.q: Her rigid food rules could suggest obsessive-compulsive disorder. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Intrusive thoughts and rituals recognised as excessive** (such as contamination or checking); weight is not the focus
**Fear of weight gain and a distorted body image**; she sees herself as too fat

nodes.q: Her weight loss could suggest hyperthyroidism. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Fast pulse, heat intolerance, tremor and a good appetite**; no fear of fatness
**Slow pulse, cold skin, restricted eating and fear of weight gain**

nodes.q: Her fainting could suggest dehydration from athletic competition. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Weight stays near normal and **potassium and acid-base balance are normal**; no body-image distress
**Starvation-level weight, amenorrhea, scarred knuckles and hypokalemic alkalosis**

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A pervasive pattern of disregard for and violation of the rights of others since age 15. The clincher: **adult (18 or older) with repeated unlawful acts, deceit, aggression and no remorse, with the pattern starting in childhood**.

nodes.q: How many of the seven DSM-5-TR criteria are needed?
nodes.note: The seven: unlawful behavior, deceitfulness, impulsivity, irritability and aggression, reckless disregard for safety, irresponsibility, and lack of remorse.

nodes.q: What is the minimum age to make the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A childhood pattern of rule breaking with onset before age 15 is also required.

nodes.q: Which cluster of personality disorders does it belong to?
nodes.note: Cluster B also includes borderline, histrionic and narcissistic personality disorders.
